If you love classic board games with a mix of strategy, adventure, and a little bit of chaos, Talisman: Digital Edition is a must-play! Nomad Games has done an excellent job bringing this legendary game to life on Steam, staying true to its tabletop roots while adding smooth digital enhancements.

The game captures the essence of Talisman perfectly—choose from a variety of unique characters, roll the dice, explore dangerous lands, and battle creatures as you race to claim the Crown of Command. The multiplayer mode is fantastic, letting you enjoy the game with friends without the hassle of setting up a physical board.

The AI is solid for single-player games, and with the variety of expansions available, there’s plenty of replayability. Whether you're a longtime Talisman fan or new to the game, this digital edition is a fantastic way to experience the magic of this classic adventure.

🔹 Pros:
✅ Faithful adaptation of the original board game
✅ Great multiplayer support (online & local)
✅ Tons of expansions for endless variety
✅ Beautifully designed board and cards

🔹 Cons:
❌ Games can be long (but that’s Talisman for you!)

Overall, Talisman: Digital Edition is a fantastic way to enjoy the classic game without worrying about lost pieces or long setup times. Highly recommended for board game lovers! 🎲🔥

This game is a masterwork in fractal complexity. Layers upon layers of interactions, secrets and mechanics. The core of the game, start to final boss, is jokingly called "the tutorial" by the comunity. And it's not much of an exaggeration, since all of the "main path" is about a 5% of the actual map.

The environment is interactable (different materials have different hardness, interacting differently to spells), the liquids have interesting effects and combine in interesting, alchemical ways. You build your own spells. 

You wield unimaginable power, and yet, the game is always one step away from killing you. Everything can (and eventually will) kill you.

Good luck, and try to start all runs getting a water flask. Between all the magical and weird liquids, water is the most valuable one for most of the game :)

I played the PS3 version of the base game back in the day and it was very good. This version seems to be pretty much the same but with some added content. Running off an SSD leads to much faster load times than running the PS3 version off an HDD.

The battle system is very good. It's most similar to Persona 3 and 4, all having systems heavily inspired by the Press Turn system introduced in Shin Megami Tensei III: Nocturne. Of course, it still bears similarity to the systems used in Persona 1 and 2, as well as most other megaten games, but not all games in the franchise work like this. Basically, in this game, if you hit an enemy's weakness (or get a critical hit), they get knocked down and you have a chance to attack again. The enemy can also do this to you. If you knock down all the enemies, you can negotiate with them to gain items, money, or take them on as the protagonist's persona in battle, taking on their strengths, weaknesses, and moveset.

In addition to the side of the game where you engage in battles, there's a strong focus on social simulation as well. Participating in the social system will benefit you in the combat side of the game and vice-versa.
The storyline was very relatable & intriguing! Thank you!

This is Diablo 1, complete rip-off of the story and everything. The difference lies in the combat, and is sadly the game's greatest weakness. The flaws show up later when they introduce new mechanics, such as monsters freezing you, and mana burn. However, the worse offender are the randomized equipment drops and how they determine your play through the game. You cannot grind for levels nor loot, so if you are unable to get items or spells that can handle dealing mass damage, the final boss is obscenely difficult to the point it felt like cheating. (I was level 26 at the time)

The final boss itself is a pushover, but it summons 5-10 monsters at a time and all them had at 7 least hit points with some using ice/fire armor. You cannot out DPS that with normal clicking, making certain cards worthless. What makes it extra frustrating is that the previous bosses don't behave like that, so you can feel determined that you're current build will work when you simply need several items like the fire axe, electric helm, a shield to reduce all the missile damage flying at you, etc etc. I would say that over half the gear becomes instantly worthless upon fighting the final boss.

There are minor flaws that irritated me, such as the user interface bars literally blocking my ability to cancel boss spells, many enemies attacking off screen where I had no ability to stop it. Still, despite the massive flaws, the game plays mostly fine. I played through it as the Warrior and I was so miffed near the halfway point, that I will not play as the other characters.

A surprisingly fun board-game in digital form. It can be played against AI, with a friend on the same pc, or through online multiplayer. The game itself is fine without any DLC - the expansions really do feel like expansions, and not bits cut out of the game.

Basically, you control one of up to six adventurers hoping to claim dominion over the land through a variety of methods - most of which include building up your strength to press into the middle of the board and reach the center square first. Every step along the way is as much RNG as it is your own choices - cards and dice, because it is, of course, a board game. Death isn't the end of the road- your character will respawn unless somebody is about to win - but if you don't like getting ♥♥♥♥♥♥ over by RNG every now and then I'd suggest avoiding this game. If you can take it in stride it adds to the fun, especially with friends.

History doesn’t repeat, but it often rhymes. When No Man's Sky was announced in 2013, the hype was so blinding that the title slipped from being a video game to a religious experience. When it finally released in 2016, a fandom that had allowed itself to be swept away reacted with absolute outrage because the game wasn't the wish-fulfilling fantasy they had dreamed up. Gamers love to forget, but for a long time, NMS was one of the most ridiculed things in the industry despite being a decent, if imperfect, title at launch.

Fast forward to 2023 and the launch of Bethesda’s long-anticipated Starfield, and this cycle of fan self-delusion rhymed perfectly. Unrealistic hype created impossible expectations, and a decent but imperfect game was promptly tarred and feathered by an internet mob outraged that reality had trumped their wild daydreams.

Despite what you might have heard, Starfield is a very good game for the discerning space gamer. Period. And with the recent Free Lanes update and Terran Armada DLC, it has only gotten better.

If you are looking for a space game that lets you play as a Jedi, you're going to want to look elsewhere; Starfield has far more in common with sober-minded space games like Elite Dangerous than it does with SWTOR. The game is built entirely on a 'NASA-punk' aesthetic, something seen in the lavishly realistic detailing adorning everything from the space suits to the interior locations. It is also a realistically grounded setting where conflict, crime, and commerce are found around the Settled Systems. Planets are realistic, from Earth-like worlds with cities to inhospitable places such as Titan or barren moons, all brought to life with orbital mechanics and weather. While initially missing (a truly mystifying omission), the recent Free Lanes update finally added intra-system travel similar to Elite’s “super-cruise”, making spaceship travel far more immersive, and providing new opportunities for exploration and encounters, both hostile and friendly.

As for the questing: there is an absolute mountain of it. I have logged over 120 hours on my current character alone (I have another 100+ on my Game Pass account!), and I still haven’t completed the main quest or any of the major faction lines. I've been completely derailed by the sheer volume of other activities, from minor character quests and outpost construction to the deep ship-building mechanics and radiant missions. Whether I'm surveying uncharted moons (now with far less repetitive PoIs) or hunting down bounties, the game always has a quick, satisfying loop ready.  On top of that, the NG+ mechanic is brilliant; instead of a simple stat-reset, it drops you into a similar yet subtly altered reality (sometimes different dialogue options, sometimes something more bizarre!), providing replayability. And none of this takes into account future official content or the many quests being added my modders.

Speaking of, while a handful of skittish modders virtue-signalled by loudly announcing they were abandoning the title, the actual modding scene is now thriving with countless mods that span the gamut from small graphical tweaks to the masterwork Kinggath Creations that rival official DLCs. There is something for everyone, in the best tradition of Bethesda titles. (And, yes, even a Star Wars mod for you space fantasy fans.)

Best of all, despite the rage-baiting doomsayers, Bethesda has not abandoned the game. They just released the Terran Armada DLC which brought some fun end-game content, and have officially announced another DLC in the works. That is one of the great things about SF: Bethesda has built such a deep sci-fi setting, truly a gaming tribute to the vast expanse of the sci-fi genre, that there are nearly limitless possibilities for future content, be it from Bethesda or modders. 

If you approach Starfield looking for an arcade popcorn experience like Borderlands, you're going to join the loud crowd of doomsayers who also got No Man's Sky wrong. But if you walk into it ready for an immersive sci-fi RPG experience and content platform - think Arma, but in space (and speaking of Arma, the gunplay is truly excellent in SF!) - you'll enjoy it and get many, many hours of entertainment.

In short, the haters got it wrong.  Again. 

Don't let them scare you away from one heck of fun ride for space gamers. Doubly-so if you like to play with mods!

Review update:

It has been over a year since I negatively reviewed this game.  Recently, I've put more time into it following numerous developer updates and content additions.  I am happy to say that the network issues and crashes have been vastly improved upon.  On the rare occassion we have a player disconnect from an online game, they can easily rejoin under 30 seconds.  I can't recall the last hard crash I had.
All DLC adds enough gameplay variety to warrant the price: getting DLC on sale is a no-brainer if you enjoy the core game.  I'd recommend two expansion board DLCs to give you enough characters, cards, and board options to make Talisman worth playing again and again.  Many of the characters make a huge difference in how the game plays and feels when you use them - I'd recommend them if you think the abilities seem interesting.

There are still a few factors that unfortunately still marr the experience: mainly UI and AI.
The game interface is made to be cross-platform with touch-screen devices.  This limits what the developers can do and is a massive drawback.  So many mechanics and things that benefit players could be improved upon by adding simple right click context or better hover info.  The game could also benefit from improvements to control, like the ability to cancel a spell (since targetting and timing of spells is still a nightmare).

With each new expansion, the AI becomes more and more prone to stupidity.  AI will take suicidal actions.  AI will waste turns.  AI can enter into infinite loops.  If you plan to play this in any single player capacity, avoid this game.  The AI alone keeps my review of this game negative.  Generally, the CPU makes 'okay' decisions. A huge problem still persists with the AI being reluctant to enter the Inner Region and attempt to win.  And the AI has no response to the strength of other players in it's decision to steup up the game, take risks, and try to stop them.
So... most AI will lose.  Unless it cheats, which it can and will...  until the dice-rolling mechanism is laid out for others to see, and not just rests on developers word, you will see that single player games are weighted against the player.  If you don't have friends, Talisman is still fun but don't expect a challenege - just enjoy the journey.

And you should enjoy it.  Talisman is fun.  The variety is there.  The multiplayer is stable and Talisman can be a wonderful game with friends online.  But the single player game is a Special Olympics simulator.

The Digital Edition of the classic Talisman board game does manage to recreate the experience pretty well, but bugs, glitches, crashes, network instability, and lack of content reflect poorly on the whole.

What does work?  The graphics are decent, without being stellar.  They get the art style across but the colors aren't vivid and lively as they are with the physical game.  The game mechanics are solid, and there are many house rules to adapt Talisman to your preferences.  Expansions are available, including one expansion board.  Playing with friends online is so much more fun... but...

What doesn't work?  Bugs that break the rules.  Glitches that can lock up the game or force things that shouldn't happen.  Poorly programmed AI that doesn't play the game well and sometimes is oblivious to things like their alignment changing (ie. now neutral characters still trying to do evil things).  The spell system is very clunky and mistakes mean you don't get to use your spells or the game uses it incorrectly and you can't cancel.  Multiplayer crashes a lot - when you can get back into the game, it inevitably locks up for everyone involved and you have to start over.  While extra content is there, it is slow to be released and is mostly of the nickel and dime variety.  Without at least one major expansion, the content in the base game will get stale quickly.  Introducing major DLC also means introducing new bugs and glitches to your game.

Bottom line is this... For a discounted price, it's a nice bit of nostalgia for people who already know and play Talisman.  I can't recommend multiplayer at this point, which is a huge disappointment.  If you're new to the game, watch some Lets Play videos of the real thing instead... and if you're still keen on Talisman, give this a shot but know about the shortcomings beforehand.
For the average off the street gamer, I can't give this a reliable thumbs up until all the glitches, bugs, and network issues are fixed.
Game is fun and the art style is unique.  Recommended, but preferably buy it on sale.

Rating: 9/10

Wasteland 3 is a masterful blend of tactical combat, deep narrative choices, and a richly detailed post-apocalyptic world that has redefined what players can expect from a modern RPG. Developed by inXile Entertainment, this third entry in the Wasteland series takes everything that made its predecessors memorable and elevates it with an intricate story, captivating characters, and improved gameplay mechanics. For both fans of the original and newcomers to the series, Wasteland 3 is a remarkable triumph.

At the heart of Wasteland 3 lies an immersive, branching narrative set in a post-apocalyptic version of Colorado. The game’s opening sets the stage for the Desert Rangers, a group of survivors tasked with maintaining some semblance of order amidst the chaos. But this time, the Rangers are called upon by the enigmatic and morally dubious Patriarch of Colorado, a leader seeking help to quash his rebellious children and unite the fractured state. As you navigate the shifting power dynamics and unravel a web of betrayal, greed, and survival, your decisions matter more than ever before.

What makes Wasteland 3 stand out in this department is its commitment to player agency. Every action, every conversation, and every alliance you form can have a profound impact on the world. The consequences are far-reaching, and they don’t always reveal themselves immediately—your decisions might come back to haunt you hours later, or even across different areas of the map. The level of depth and the weight of player choice makes Wasteland 3 feel truly dynamic, offering a personalized experience that keeps you on your toes.

Tactical combat in Wasteland 3 is an absolute treat. The game adopts a turn-based system, where positioning, cover, and skillful use of your squad’s unique abilities are essential to success. The combat is demanding, rewarding, and offers a satisfying sense of accomplishment when you outsmart your enemies. The AI presents a solid challenge, but it’s the variety of approaches you can take that makes combat so engaging. You’ll find yourself experimenting with different character builds and strategies, as each encounter provides a new puzzle to solve.

Wasteland 3 is a triumph in almost every sense. It delivers a rich, immersive world filled with memorable characters, tough moral choices, and challenging tactical combat. The game builds on the foundation set by its predecessors and refines it in every way, creating a captivating RPG experience that is both rewarding and thought-provoking. Whether you're a long-time fan of the Wasteland series or someone just discovering it, this is an experience you won't want to miss.
